extracted.intended_audience: general readers, legal and public-health researchers, policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: A compact summary and extraction of the substantive provisions, obligations, adjustments, enforcement mechanisms, and criticisms found in the 1998 Tobacco Master Settlement Agreement (MSA) as described on the Wikipedia page. Useful for readers seeking the agreement's key legal/financial/regulatory standards and implementation features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on youth targeting
rubrics_metrics.description: Participating manufacturers agreed not to 'take any action, directly or indirectly, to target Youth within any Settling State in the advertising, promotion or marketing of Tobacco Products, or take any action the primary purpose of which is to initiate, maintain or increase the incidence of Youth smoking within any Settling State.' (§III(a))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specified bans include outdoor billboards, advertising on transit vehicles, restrictions on sports marketing, event sponsorship, and promotional products. This is broad language prohibiting actions whose primary purpose is to target youth; enforcement provisions and examples are included elsewhere in the agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad limits on advertising, sponsorship, lobbying, and litigation activities
rubrics_metrics.description: The Original Participating Manufacturers agreed to restrict their advertising, sponsorship, lobbying, and litigation activities, particularly where such activities were seen as targeting youth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This general limitation complements the explicit youth-targeting prohibition and supports other specific advertising/sponsorship bans and dissolution/restriction of industry organizations (see related entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Disbandment and restriction of tobacco-related organizations
rubrics_metrics.description: The OPMs agreed to disband three specific 'Tobacco-Related Organizations' and to restrict their creation and participation in trade associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agreement led to dissolution of the Tobacco Institute, Center for Indoor Air Research, and the Council for Tobacco Research; it also restricts future formation/participation in similar organizations as an MSA obligation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public disclosure of discovery documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The OPMs agreed generally to make available to the public documents the OPMs had disclosed during the discovery phase of litigation with the settling states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MSA created a public document archive (e.g., Truth Initiative archive) and required ongoing availability of many internal industry documents disclosed in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation and funding of national public education entities
rubrics_metrics.description: The agreement required creation/funding of organizations dedicated to reducing youth smoking and preventing smoking-related disease (e.g., National Public Education Foundation; Truth Initiative created from the MSA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial contributions and specific funds (National Foundation, Public Education Fund) are enumerated elsewhere; the MSA's public-education obligations are intended to support anti-smoking programs but criticisms note underfunding of prevention efforts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpetual annual payments to settling states
rubrics_metrics.description: Participating Manufacturers agreed to make annual payments to the settling states in perpetuity; the MSA committed at least $206 billion over the first 25 years (with detailed payment schedules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payments include up-front payments, estimated annual payments through 2025, and other designated funds (Strategic Contribution Fund, National Foundation, Public Education Fund, State Enforcement Fund, NAAG payments). Payments are subject to numerous adjustments and offsets (see Payment Adjustments entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: OPM payment calculation: relative market share and Volume Adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: For Original Participating Manufacturers (OPMs), payments are determined in accordance with their relative market share as of 1997 and are subject to a 'Volume Adjustment' comparing current cigarette sales to 1997 sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an OPM sells fewer cigarettes in a payment year than in 1997, the Volume Adjustment can reduce that OPM's payment. The MSA sets baseline annual amounts apportioned by each OPM's Relative Market Share for the preceding year. See 'Relative Market Share' definition for measurement details.

rubrics_metrics.name: SPM joining rules and 90-day exemption (Subsequent Participating Manufacturers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subsequent Participating Manufacturers (SPMs) who joined within 90 days of the MSA's execution were exempt from making annual payments unless they increased market share beyond specified historic thresholds; SPMs joining after 90 days must pay based on all national cigarette sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exempt SPMs only pay if sales exceed either the SPM's 1998 market share or 125% of its 1997 market share. Non-exempt SPMs must, after joining, pay amounts equivalent to what they would have owed from the execution date until their joining date. Payment calculations for SPMs use the OPM market-share denominator (see guidance on denominators).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and measurement of 'Relative Market Share'
rubrics_metrics.description: The MSA defines 'Relative Market Share' as an OPM's percentage share of total cigarettes shipped to the 50 states, DC, and Puerto Rico during the calendar year preceding the payment year, as measured by reports to Management Science Associates (or successor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The definition includes measurement rules (e.g., 0.09 ounces roll-your-own tobacco equals one individual cigarette) and tie-breaking conventions (a cigarette shipped by more than one PM deemed shipped by the first PM). These measurement rules directly affect payment allocations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payment adjustments and offsets affecting annual payments
rubrics_metrics.description: MSA baseline payments are subject to multiple adjustments and offsets including the Inflation Adjustment, Volume Adjustment, Previously Settled States Reduction, Non-Settling States Reduction, NPM Adjustment, offsets for miscalculated or disputed payments, Federal Tobacco Legislation Offset, Litigating Releasing Parties Offset, and offsets for claims overdrafts (subsections XII etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These adjustments can materially change amounts received by states; they are defined in the MSA text and referenced throughout the implementation discussion. Disputes and recalculations are possible under the agreement's mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escrow account and model/qualifying escrow act
rubrics_metrics.description: Payments from PMs (and required payments from NPMs) are deposited into escrow accounts until disbursement to settling states; the MSA includes a model escrow (qualifying) act and incentivizes states to adopt it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'Qualifying Statute' neutralizes cost disadvantages versus NPMs; adoption prevents the state's share being reduced by the NPM Adjustment. All settling states enacted qualifying statutes. The model statute prescribes per-cigarette escrow amounts and enforcement mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: NPM (Nonparticipating Manufacturer) obligations and escrow payments
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-Participating Manufacturers must either join the MSA or make annual escrow payments (liability reserve) into a state escrow account; escrow funds may only be used to pay judgments/settlements against the NPM and revert after 25 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Escrow payments are calculated by multiplying a per-cigarette amount (set by each state's legislature/model statute) by cigarettes sold in the state that year. The MSA and model statutes set specific per-unit amounts for given years (detailed year-by-year rates are provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: NPM Adjustment and state safe-harbor/enforcement obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPM Adjustment allows a state's allocated MSA payment to be reduced if PMs lose market share due to NPMs and an economic consultant determines the MSA was a significant factor; a state can avoid this reduction by enacting and diligently enforcing the model qualifying/escrow statute (safe harbor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates an incentive for states to adopt and enforce model escrow laws and for complementary legislation to compel compliance. The NPM Adjustment ties state receipts to controlling NPM market-share impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocable Share distribution to states
rubrics_metrics.description: Each settling state receives an 'Allocable Share' — a preset percentage of the funds held in escrow agreed upon by the settling states — and this Allocable Share does not vary according to cigarettes sold in that particular state in a given year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus distribution among states is fixed by allocable percentages rather than per-state sales volumes; this fact created policy and loophole implications for escrow/refund rules discussed in the ASR Repealer section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocable Share Release and ASR Repealer (refund rules for NPM escrow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally, escrow statutes authorized an early release/refund of escrow amounts greater than a state's allocable share; this created loopholes when NPMs concentrated sales regionally. NAAG introduced the Allocable Share Release Repealer to remove that refund method and revise refund calculations so refunds are compared to what an NPM would have paid under the MSA for those units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ASR Repealer revised refund calculation to remove enacting state's 'allocable share' reference and instead compares escrowed funds to the MSA payment that would have been owed for those units, closing the regional-sales loophole. Practical implementation details and case law followed (see related citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement mechanisms and state enforcement fund
rubrics_metrics.description: The MSA gives jurisdiction to individual state courts to implement and enforce terms and established a State Enforcement Fund (one-time payment of $50 million); participating manufacturers also paid states' attorney fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enforcement provisions include remedies available to states and the institutional funding to support enforcement actions. Complementary state statutes and litigation have further shaped enforcement practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase II settlement for tobacco growers and related trust fund
rubrics_metrics.description: A subsequent Phase II settlement compensated tobacco growers expected to suffer due to higher cigarette prices; it created the National Tobacco Growers' Settlement Trust Fund and defined eligibility for growers/quota holders in specified flue-cured and burley tobacco states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a distinct MSA-related agreement addressing agricultural impacts and distributing payments to growers and quota holders in listed states; it establishes eligibility rules and payment mechanics separate from the PM/state payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use/allocation of MSA proceeds and criticisms about spending priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: The MSA designated various funds and payments (up-front, annual, Strategic Contribution Fund, National Foundation, Public Education Fund, State Enforcement Fund, NAAG payments), but critics say too little of MSA money has been spent on tobacco prevention and anti-smoking measures and some states used funds for unrelated purposes (budget holes, golf courses, industry subsidies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry captures the evaluative criterion applied by public-health advocates and commentators: adequacy and appropriation of MSA proceeds toward tobacco control. Empirical details (e.g., less than 3% spent on tobacco prevention at some points; as of 2020 >$138B paid) are cited in the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Securitization (tobacco bonds) and fiscal/risk implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Many states securitized future MSA payments by issuing 'tobacco bonds' to transfer revenue risk to bondholders; declining tobacco revenue and growth of e-cigarettes have reduced expected payments and led to downgrades, technical defaults, and predicted defaults for some bonds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates fiscal risks and perverse incentives (states reliant on future tobacco revenue may have incentives to protect the tobacco industry); proposals to tax e-cigarettes to offset declines are discussed. This is a policy-evaluation standard regarding whether securitization preserves or undermines public-interest goals.
